title: Older Adult Medication Reconciliation: Include OTCs, Supplements, and Actual Use
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Polypharmacy risk cannot be assessed from the prescription list alone. Reconcile what the older adult actually takes, including OTC products, supplements, duplicate products, skipped doses, and medications from multiple prescribers.
recognize: Multiple pharmacies/prescribers, cognitive impairment, low health literacy, recent discharge, and pillbox confusion increase discrepancy risk.
priorities: Build one accurate medication list and escalate duplicate therapy, interactions, unclear indications, or high-risk symptoms.
assessMonitor: Medication name/strength/timing, indication, prescriber, adherence, renal/hepatic function, falls, cognition, dizziness, and bleeding/sedation symptoms.
interventions: Use teach-back, updated written lists, pharmacy collaboration, and simplified routines when prescribed.
medicationSafety: Do not independently discontinue chronic medication because it appears unnecessary; route concerns for medication review.
teaching: Carry an updated list including vitamins, herbals, and OTC drugs.
delegationScope: Medication-history collection may be shared; discrepancy interpretation requires licensed review.
examTrap: Accepting the electronic medication list as accurate without asking what the patient actually takes.
oneLinePearl: The safest medication list is the one that matches real use.
sourceBasis: FDA medication safety tips for older adults

title: New Confusion After Medication Change: Treat as Possible Adverse Effect or Delirium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: New confusion, somnolence, hallucinations, or agitation after a medication change may reflect drug toxicity, interaction, withdrawal, infection, hypoxia, metabolic illness, or pain. Do not assume dementia progression.
recognize: Recent sedative, opioid, anticholinergic, steroid, antihistamine, or dose changes are important clues.
priorities: Assess ABCs, vitals, glucose/oxygenation as indicated, recent medication changes, and other delirium triggers.
assessMonitor: Attention, level of consciousness, medication timing, renal function, hydration, urine/stool retention, pain, and infection cues.
interventions: Notify the provider/pharmacist and use nonpharmacologic delirium supports while the cause is evaluated.
medicationSafety: Do not add another sedating medication simply to suppress behavior before evaluating the cause.
teaching: Families should report abrupt cognitive changes, especially after medication changes.
delegationScope: Behavior observation may be delegated; acute-change interpretation requires licensed judgment.
oneLinePearl: New confusion in an older adult is a change in condition, not a normal age effect.

title: Fall After Medication Change: Review Drugs and Physiology Together
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A new fall after medication initiation or dose change should trigger assessment for orthostasis, sedation, hypoglycemia, bleeding, bradycardia, and drug interactions—not only environmental fall prevention.
recognize: Antihypertensives, sedatives, opioids, hypoglycemics, and drugs with anticholinergic effects can contribute depending on context.
priorities: Assess injury first, then physiologic and medication contributors.
assessMonitor: Orthostatic symptoms/BP if appropriate, pulse, glucose if indicated, neuro status, pain, bleeding, gait, and medication timing.
interventions: Institute fall precautions and escalate suspected medication-related contributors for review.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop chronic cardiovascular or CNS medications without clinical review unless an emergency protocol directs otherwise.
teaching: Rise slowly, use prescribed mobility aids, and report dizziness or excessive sleepiness.
delegationScope: Fall-risk precautions may be delegated; post-fall clinical interpretation is licensed.
examTrap: Blaming the rug while ignoring a newly doubled sedative dose.
oneLinePearl: After a fall, inspect the medication list as carefully as the environment.

title: Anticholinergic Burden: Dry Mouth, Retention, Constipation, and Confusion Can Cluster
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Multiple medications with anticholinergic effects can collectively worsen confusion, constipation, urinary retention, dry mouth, blurred vision, and falls in older adults. Review the whole regimen rather than one drug at a time.
recognize: New retention, constipation, delirium, dry mouth, and blurred vision after medication additions are clues.
priorities: Assess symptom severity and medication burden and route concerns for prescriber/pharmacist review.
assessMonitor: Cognition, bowel/bladder pattern, hydration, vision, falls, and recent OTC antihistamine/sleep-aid use.
interventions: Use non-drug comfort measures and reinforce safer prescribed alternatives when the plan changes.
medicationSafety: Many OTC sleep/allergy products add anticholinergic burden and may be missed unless specifically asked about.
teaching: Check with a clinician/pharmacist before adding OTC sleep or allergy medicines.
delegationScope: Symptom collection may be delegated; medication-risk synthesis is licensed.
examTrap: Treating each symptom with another medication without considering a shared drug cause.
oneLinePearl: Polypharmacy can create a syndrome, not just isolated side effects.

title: Declining Renal Function: A Previously Safe Dose Can Become Toxic
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Age-related and acute changes in kidney function can increase exposure to renally cleared medications. New sedation, confusion, bleeding, bradycardia, or other toxicity cues after dehydration or AKI require medication review.
recognize: Vomiting, poor intake, infection, diuresis, and new AKI can abruptly change drug clearance.
priorities: Assess renal trend, hydration, medication timing, and toxicity symptoms; notify the provider/pharmacist.
assessMonitor: Creatinine/eGFR trend as ordered, urine output, weight/hydration, and drug-specific toxicity signs.
interventions: Support ordered hydration and dose/interval adjustment plans.
medicationSafety: Do not assume a longstanding dose remains appropriate after renal function changes.
teaching: Report dehydration or major illness because some medicines may require clinician review.
delegationScope: I/O and routine labs may be collected by team members; medication-toxicity interpretation is licensed.
examTrap: Reassuring the patient because the same dose was tolerated for years.
oneLinePearl: A stable dose can become unstable when kidney function changes.

title: Deprescribing Awareness: More Medications Is Not Always Safer
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Medication review should ask whether each drug still has an indication, benefit, acceptable burden, and safe interaction profile. The PN/LVN identifies concerns and reinforces the plan; prescribing or deprescribing remains authorized prescriber work.
recognize: Duplicate classes, medications without clear indication, high pill burden, poor adherence, recurrent adverse effects, and changing goals of care are review cues.
priorities: Clarify indication and actual use and route concerns for interdisciplinary review.
assessMonitor: Symptoms, treatment goals, adherence, adverse effects, functional status, and patient preferences.
interventions: Reinforce tapering/monitoring instructions exactly as prescribed and watch for withdrawal or symptom recurrence.
medicationSafety: Some medications require tapering and should not be abruptly stopped.
complications: Adverse drug events if unnecessary therapy continues
teaching: Medication reduction should be planned with the prescriber, not done independently.
delegationScope: The PN/LVN can identify and communicate medication burden; prescribing authority is jurisdiction-specific and generally outside PN scope.
examTrap: Stopping a long-term medication immediately because it seems unnecessary.
oneLinePearl: Deprescribing is a clinical plan, not a pill-count exercise.

title: Older Adult on Anticoagulants: Subtle Bleeding and Falls Need Respect
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Anticoagulants reduce thrombotic risk but increase bleeding risk. New weakness, melena, hematuria, unexplained bruising, hypotension, falling hemoglobin, or head trauma after a fall needs prompt evaluation.
recognize: Renal decline, interacting drugs, duplicate antithrombotics, and adherence errors can increase risk.
priorities: Assess hemodynamics, bleeding sites, medication list, timing of last dose, and recent falls/trauma.
assessMonitor: BP/HR, neuro status after head trauma, stool/urine, bruising, CBC/renal function and drug-specific labs as ordered.
interventions: Apply local bleeding control and escalate for reversal/diagnostic decisions.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop or reverse anticoagulation unless an emergency protocol/order authorizes it.
complications: Thrombosis if therapy is inappropriately stopped
teaching: Report bleeding and falls promptly and avoid unapproved NSAID/OTC interactions.
delegationScope: Bleeding observation may be delegated; anticoagulant management is licensed/provider directed.
examTrap: Ignoring a minor-looking head bump because there is no external bleeding.
oneLinePearl: On anticoagulation, hidden bleeding matters more than bruise size.

title: Older Adult With Diabetes: Hypoglycemia May Present as Confusion or Falls
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hypoglycemia in older adults may present as confusion, weakness, behavior change, or a fall rather than classic adrenergic symptoms. Check glucose promptly when clinically appropriate, especially after poor intake or medication changes.
recognize: Insulin, sulfonylureas, missed meals, renal decline, weight loss, and acute illness increase risk.
priorities: Check glucose when indicated and treat confirmed hypoglycemia per protocol while evaluating the cause.
assessMonitor: Glucose trend, meal intake, renal function, medication timing/dose, cognition, and recurrence.
interventions: Use protocolized oral or parenteral glucose treatment based on consciousness/swallow safety.
medicationSafety: Repeated episodes require prescriber review of the diabetes regimen rather than simply adding snacks indefinitely.
teaching: Link medication timing to meals and know the individualized low-glucose action plan.
delegationScope: Glucose checks/treatment may be delegated only per policy; recurrent-cause analysis is licensed.
examTrap: Calling new confusion dementia before checking glucose in an at-risk patient.
oneLinePearl: In older adults, hypoglycemia can look like delirium or a fall.

title: Dehydration Plus Medications: Watch for AKI, Orthostasis, and Toxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Poor intake, vomiting, fever, or diuresis can interact with antihypertensives, diuretics, diabetes medicines, and renally cleared drugs. New orthostasis, oliguria, weakness, or confusion requires evaluation of both hydration and medication effects.
recognize: Dry mouth may be unreliable when medications cause it; trend urine, weight, BP, intake, and function.
priorities: Assess perfusion/hydration and reconcile medications in the context of the acute illness.
assessMonitor: Intake/output, weight, orthostatic symptoms, BP/HR, renal/electrolyte labs as ordered, and medication timing.
interventions: Support prescribed fluid plan and route medication concerns for sick-day review.
medicationSafety: Do not independently apply generic 'sick-day' medication holds; plans are medication/patient specific.
teaching: During acute illness, contact the care team if intake is poor or dizziness/low urine develops.
delegationScope: I/O and weights may be delegated; medication/AKI interpretation requires licensed review.
examTrap: Treating dizziness only with fall precautions while ignoring dehydration and medication effects.
oneLinePearl: Acute illness can turn routine medications into new risks.

title: OTC Medications in Older Adults: 'Nonprescription' Does Not Mean Low Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: OTC sleep aids, antihistamines, NSAIDs, decongestants, laxatives, and combination cold products can interact with chronic disease and prescriptions. Always include OTC use in medication review.
recognize: Confusion, dry mouth, retention, constipation, bleeding, BP elevation, edema, and duplicate acetaminophen are common preventable patterns depending on the product.
priorities: Ask specifically about OTCs and supplements and check labels for duplicate ingredients/interactions.
assessMonitor: Cognition, bowel/bladder function, BP, edema, renal function, bleeding, and total daily ingredient exposure as relevant.
interventions: Reinforce pharmacist/provider review before adding OTC products to a complex regimen.
medicationSafety: Brand names can hide multiple active ingredients; review the ingredient list.
teaching: Bring OTCs and supplements to medication reviews, not just prescriptions.
delegationScope: Medication-list collection can be shared; interaction assessment is licensed/pharmacist work.
examTrap: Assuming a pharmacy-shelf medication cannot meaningfully interact with prescriptions.
oneLinePearl: OTC is a purchase category, not a safety category.
sourceBasis: FDA medication safety tips for older adults
